text: Most of the harm in this story did not start with a mob.
It started with a number.
In 1933 the University of Chicago Press published a thick book called One Hundred Years of Land Values in Chicago.
The author was an economist named Homer Hoyt, and the book had begun as his doctoral dissertation here at the University of Chicago.
It runs more than five hundred pages.
It tracks the price of Chicago dirt, block by block, from 1830 to 1933.
Hoyt was a careful man with numbers.
He had a law degree and a doctorate, and he could read a city the way a doctor reads an x ray.
Most of the book is dry, page after page of tables and curves.
One table is not.
In that table Hoyt ranked races and nationalities by their supposed effect on land values.
At the top he put English, Germans, Scots, Irish, and Scandinavians.
Below them, North Italians.
Then Bohemians, Poles, Lithuanians, Greeks.
Near the bottom he placed Russian Jews of the lower class and South Italians.
At the very bottom he wrote Negroes, and then Mexicans.
Hoyt added a note that mattered.
The other groups, he wrote, would blend in once they rose in income and lived like Americans.
For Black and Mexican residents, he said, that door stayed closed.
He had taken an old prejudice and dressed it as economics.
The table did not read like hate.
It read like a footnote, calm and precise, which is exactly what made it dangerous.
A banker could cite it.
A judge could cite it.
An appraiser could fold it into a formula and never feel the cruelty of it.
